title: Develop a harvesting plan for the specific agricultural crop

lessons.title: Information needed for a harvesting plan
lessons.html:
Purpose of a harvesting plan

A harvesting plan sets out when, where, how and by whom a crop will be harvested, and how it will be handled and delivered, so that the maximum volume of product reaches the market at the required quality and at the lowest cost. It is written for a specific crop because maturity indicators, handling and market requirements differ greatly between, for example, citrus, table grapes, potatoes, maize and leafy vegetables.

Crop information

  • Blocks, cultivars, hectares and planting dates
  • Yield estimates from crop counts, sample weighing or historical records, updated as harvest approaches
  • Expected harvest window per block, based on cultivar, climate and maturity tests
  • Spray records and pre-harvest intervals from product labels for every block

Maturity and quality standards

Define the indicators for the crop and market: colour, size, firmness, sugar to acid ratio, Brix, dry matter (avocados), grain moisture, skin set (potatoes). Include the buyer's or export specifications and tolerances.

Market requirements

  • Delivery programmes: volumes per week, packing format, labels
  • Certification requirements, such as GAP schemes
  • Transport arrangements and lead times

Resources

  • Labour: number of pickers, team leaders, quality controllers; training needs; accommodation and transport
  • Equipment: picking bags, crates, bins, ladders, clippers, trailers, forklifts, combine harvesters, diggers
  • Packhouse or silo capacity per day, cold storage capacity
  • Budget for labour, fuel, packaging and transport

Constraints

Weather risks (rain at harvest, heat), public holidays, competition for labour from neighbouring farms, packhouse bottlenecks and road conditions must all be considered.

lessons.title: Writing and running the harvesting plan
lessons.html:
Building the schedule

  1. List blocks in order of expected maturity, confirmed by maturity tests.
  2. Calculate daily capacity: pickers multiplied by output per picker per day, limited by packhouse, transport or machine capacity.
  3. Divide each block's estimated yield by daily capacity to get the number of harvest days.
  4. Place blocks on a calendar, allowing for weather days, maintenance and holidays.
  5. Check that no block is scheduled before its pre-harvest interval ends.

Operating procedures in the plan

  • Picking method and standards, with photos of acceptable product
  • Handling: maximum crate fill, shade at collection points, time to cooling
  • Hygiene: handwashing, toilets, illness reporting, clean containers
  • Traceability: bin or crate tickets with block, date and team
  • Quality control sampling at field and intake
  • Safety: ladders, lifting, heat stress, machinery and transport of workers

Contingency plans

  • Rain: which blocks can be picked after rain, drying requirements
  • Breakdowns: backup equipment or contractor arrangements
  • Labour shortage: priority blocks, overtime within legal limits
  • Market changes: alternative buyers or storage options

Communication and monitoring

Share the plan with team leaders, the packhouse, transport and sales. Hold daily planning meetings, track actual volumes against the plan, and update yield estimates and the schedule as harvest progresses.

Review

After the season, compare planned and actual dates, volumes, quality, costs and incidents. Record lessons for next year's plan.

Key points

  • Base the plan on yield estimates, maturity indicators and market programmes.
  • Always respect pre-harvest intervals from labels.
  • Calculate harvest days from yield and the limiting capacity.
  • Include handling, hygiene, traceability, quality and safety procedures.
  • Prepare contingencies, track progress daily and review after the season.
